scenes.head: Diversification
scenes.sub: Measure how two investments move together with covariance and correlation, work out the risk of a portfolio, and see how much risk spreading money removes, how much it can’t, and when it lets you down.

segs.say: Diversification. Measure how two investments move together with covariance and correlation, work out the risk of a portfolio, and see how much risk spreading money removes, how much it can’t, and when it lets you down.

scenes.head: You will be able to

segs.say: Calculate the covariance and correlation of two assets’ returns, from scenarios and from history, and interpret them.
Calculate the expected return and standard deviation of a two-asset portfolio and find the mix with the least risk.
Explain why a portfolio’s standard deviation is below the weighted average of its parts unless the correlation is 1.
Distinguish systematic from unsystematic risk and estimate how a portfolio’s risk falls as holdings are added.
Evaluate how well diversification held up in the simulated crashes of 2020 and 2022, and what correlation can and can’t promise.

scenes.head: June 2028.

segs.say: June 2028. Ana Lim has opened a retirement account: $5,000 from her parents on 1 July and $400 a month after that, for about 30 years. Her provider offers three Harbourline index funds (total market, international and bonds) and an actively managed fund. Her first instinct is to put everything in the total-market fund, which earned the most over the last fifteen years. Her second is to ask why anyone holds a bond fund that earned less than half as much. This lesson answers the second question, and in doing so explains why the total-market fund itself is a good idea.

scenes.head: A portfolio is the set of investments someone holds.

segs.say: A portfolio is the set of investments someone holds. Each holding’s portfolio weight is its share of the total value: $6,000 in shares and $4,000 in bonds is a 60% weight in shares and 40% in bonds. The weights add up to 1. A portfolio’s return in any period is simply the weighted average of its holdings’ returns. If shares return 10% and bonds 4%, the 60/40 portfolio returns 0.6 × 10% + 0.4 × 4% = 7.6%. Expected return works the same way.

scenes.head: Risk does not.

segs.say: Risk does not. The standard deviation of a portfolio is usually less than the weighted average of its holdings’ standard deviations, because when one holding has a bad month the others often don’t, and the losses are partly offset. That is diversification: spreading money across investments that don’t move in lockstep. How much it helps depends on one thing only, beyond the holdings’ own risks: how closely they move together. This lesson measures that with covariance and the correlation coefficient.

scenes.head: The figures in this course’s market history are simulated for teaching: monthly total returns for January 2013 to December 2027, generated to look…

segs.say: The figures in this course’s market history are simulated for teaching: monthly total returns for January 2013 to December 2027, generated to look broadly like real markets, for fictional funds and companies. They are not real history. For real long-run returns, check a source such as Aswath Damodaran’s annually updated table of US stock, bond and bill returns since 1928 (see the references).
The Harbourline funds, January 2013 – December 2027 (simulated monthly returns, annualised)

scenes.head: The bond fund’s correlation with the share market is low, 0.32, so in many months when shares fell the bond fund held its value or rose.

segs.say: The bond fund’s correlation with the share market is low, 0.32, so in many months when shares fell the bond fund held its value or rose. That is what makes it worth holding alongside shares even though its own return is lower. The international fund is a different case: its correlation with the home market is 0.78, so it moves with home shares much of the time and diversifies less.

scenes.head: Return averages; risk doesn’t

segs.say: Return averages; risk doesn’t. A portfolio’s expected return is the weighted average of its holdings’ expected returns. Its standard deviation is below the weighted average of their standard deviations whenever their correlation is less than 1. The gap is the free lunch of diversification: less risk for the same expected return.

scenes.head: Covariance measures whether two returns tend to be above their means at the same time.

segs.say: Covariance measures whether two returns tend to be above their means at the same time. For each period, multiply the two assets’ deviations from their own means; the covariance is the average of those products (dividing by n − 1 for a sample, as Excel’s COVARIANCE.S does). If both tend to be above average together and below average together, most products are positive and so is the covariance. If one tends to be up when the other is down, it is negative.

scenes.head: Covariance is hard to read on its own because its units are the product of the two returns’ units (per cent squared, per month squared).

segs.say: Covariance is hard to read on its own because its units are the product of the two returns’ units (per cent squared, per month squared). Dividing it by the two standard deviations gives the correlation coefficient, ρ (rho), a pure number from −1 to +1: +1 when the two always move in exact proportion in the same direction, −1 when they always move in exact proportion in opposite directions, and 0 when there is no straight-line relation at all. Correlation describes co-movement; it does not say that one asset causes the other’s moves.

scenes.head: For the simulated history, the total-market fund’s monthly standard deviation is 4.62% and the bond fund’s 1.19%.

segs.say: For the simulated history, the total-market fund’s monthly standard deviation is 4.62% and the bond fund’s 1.19%. Their monthly covariance is 0.000177, so their correlation is 0.000177 ÷ (0.0462 × 0.0119) = 0.32. Annualised, the covariance is 12 × 0.000177 = 0.00213; the correlation is the same in monthly and annual units, because the factor of 12 multiplies the covariance and the product of the two standard deviations alike.

scenes.head: With scenarios instead of history, use probabilities in place of the equal weights: the covariance is Σₛ pₛ (r_(A,s) − E[r_A])(r_(B,s) − E[r_B])…

segs.say: With scenarios instead of history, use probabilities in place of the equal weights: the covariance is Σₛ pₛ (r_(A,s) − E[r_A])(r_(B,s) − E[r_B]), with no n − 1. The worked examples do one.

chapters.title: The risk of a two-asset portfolio

scenes.head: With a weight w in asset A and 1 − w in asset B, the portfolio’s variance is

segs.say: With a weight w in asset A and 1 − w in asset B, the portfolio’s variance is
σ_P² = w²σ_A² + (1 − w)²σ_B² + 2 w(1 − w) ρ_(AB) σ_Aσ_B

scenes.head: The first two terms are each asset’s own risk, scaled by the square of its weight.

segs.say: The first two terms are each asset’s own risk, scaled by the square of its weight. The third is the interaction, and it is where diversification lives: it carries the correlation (ρ_(AB)σ_Aσ_B is just the covariance). The lower the correlation, the smaller the third term, and below zero it subtracts.

scenes.head: For Ana’s two candidate funds, a mix of 60% total market and 40% bonds has an expected return of 0.6 × 10.43% + 0.4 × 4.31% = 7.98% a year.

segs.say: For Ana’s two candidate funds, a mix of 60% total market and 40% bonds has an expected return of 0.6 × 10.43% + 0.4 × 4.31% = 7.98% a year. Its variance is the sum of three terms, 0.36 × 0.1600², 0.16 × 0.0414² and 2 × 0.24 × 0.32 × 0.1600 × 0.0414, which come to 0.0105, so its standard deviation is √0.0105 = 10.25%. The weighted average of the two standard deviations is 0.6 × 16.00% + 0.4 × 4.14% = 11.25%, so diversification removes 1.00 point of risk without costing any expected return. The formula is exact for the sample: the actual month-by-month returns of a 60/40 mix, rebalanced every month, have the same 10.25%.
Mixes of the total-market and bond funds (simulated 2013–2027, correlation 0.32)

scenes.head: Three cases mark out the possibilities.

segs.say: Three cases mark out the possibilities. When ρ = + 1, the formula collapses to σ_P = wσ_A + (1 − w)σ_B: the standard deviation is the weighted average and diversification achieves nothing. When ρ = −1, the two always move against each other and there is a mix with no risk at all, w = σ_B ÷ (σ_A + σ_B): for these two funds, 20.5% in shares. Real assets sit between. Every correlation below 1 gives some reduction, and the lower the correlation, the larger it is. The Explore widget lets you drag the correlation and watch the curve of mixes bend.

scenes.head: Setting the derivative of the variance to zero gives the weight in A with the least risk:

segs.say: Setting the derivative of the variance to zero gives the weight in A with the least risk:
w^* = (σ_B² − ρ_(AB)σ_Aσ_B)/(σ_A² + σ_B² − 2ρ_(AB)σ_Aσ_B)

scenes.head: For the total-market and bond funds it gives w^* = −1.8%: the least risky mix would sell shares short.

segs.say: For the total-market and bond funds it gives w^* = −1.8%: the least risky mix would sell shares short. Without short selling, the least risky portfolio is 100% bonds. That happens whenever the correlation is above the ratio of the smaller standard deviation to the larger (here 0.0414 ÷ 0.1600 = 0.26): adding a little of a much riskier asset that moves partly with the safe one adds more risk than it removes. Had the correlation been 0, the least risky mix would have held 6.3% in shares. So a little of a risky asset can reduce risk, but only if it is not too correlated with what you already hold.

scenes.head: Two shares of similar risk give a more interesting answer.

segs.say: Two shares of similar risk give a more interesting answer. Morrow & Pike Roasters and Harbour Street Foods, two of the course’s fictional listed companies, have standard deviations of 25.25% and 32.03% a year in the simulated history and a correlation of 0.35. Half in each has an expected return of 11.06% and a standard deviation of 23.61%, well below the 28.64% average of the two. The least risky mix holds 67.7% in Morrow & Pike, with a standard deviation of 22.88%. Notice that every one of these two-share portfolios is still far riskier than the total-market fund (16.00%), which earned about the same.

chapters.title: Many assets: the risk that diversification can’t remove

scenes.head: Add more holdings and the pattern continues, up to a limit.

segs.say: Add more holdings and the pattern continues, up to a limit. For an equally weighted portfolio of n assets, each with the same average variance and the same average covariance with the others, the portfolio variance is
σ_P² = 1/n σ²̄ + (1 − 1/n)cov̄

scenes.head: As n grows, the first term, each holding’s own risk, shrinks towards zero: that is unsystematic risk, the part specific to each company, being…

segs.say: As n grows, the first term, each holding’s own risk, shrinks towards zero: that is unsystematic risk, the part specific to each company, being diversified away. The second term tends to the average covariance and stays. That is systematic risk, the part every share shares because they all respond to the same economy. No amount of spreading within shares removes it.

scenes.head: Suppose typical shares are like Morrow & Pike and Harbour Street: an average variance of 0.0832 a year (a standard deviation of 28.84%) and an…

segs.say: Suppose typical shares are like Morrow & Pike and Harbour Street: an average variance of 0.0832 a year (a standard deviation of 28.84%) and an average covariance of 0.0283. The table shows what equal weighting does. Most of the reduction comes from the first ten or so holdings, and the floor, √0.0283 = 16.83%, is close to the total-market fund’s own 16.00%: the market fund has already diversified away almost all the specific risk. OpenStax’s Principles of Finance (section 15.2) makes the same point with real shares: risk falls quickly at first and then slowly. It notes that there is no exact number, but that “the average investor can create a reasonably diversified portfolio with approximately a dozen stocks.”
Standard deviation of an equally weighted portfolio of n typical shares (average variance 0.0832, average covariance 0.0283; simulated)

scenes.head: This is why the market pays no premium for unsystematic risk: anyone can get rid of it cheaply.

segs.say: This is why the market pays no premium for unsystematic risk: anyone can get rid of it cheaply. The simulated history is consistent with this, though it can’t prove it: Morrow & Pike’s standard deviation (25.25%) was far above the market fund’s (16.00%) but its mean return was lower (9.59% against 10.43%). With a standard error of about 6.5 points on a fifteen-year mean, and Harbour Street earning more than the market (12.53%), single shares’ averages are too noisy to be evidence either way. The CAPM lesson turns this into a rule: expected return depends only on the systematic part of risk, measured by beta. To remove systematic risk you have to hold something outside the share market, such as bonds or bills, and accept a lower expected return.

scenes.head: Correlations are not fixed.

segs.say: Correlations are not fixed. A common observation in real markets is that shares in different countries and industries fall together in a crash, just when diversification is wanted most. The simulated data show it clearly for 2020 and show why. Measured within single calendar years, Morrow & Pike and Harbour Street had their highest correlation of the fifteen years in 2020 (0.78, against 0.35 over the whole period), and the home and international funds their second highest (0.90, against 0.78). In March 2020 one shock, a 17% fall in the market, hit every share at once, and a common shock that large dominates the year’s movements. 2022’s share correlations (0.85 and 0.49) were higher than the fifteen-year figures but within the normal year-to-year range: the home–international correlation was 0.91 in 2025, a good year. Twelve-month estimates are too noisy to establish the crash pattern; that claim rests on real-market studies, not on this simulation.
Correlations of monthly returns within a calendar year (simulated)

scenes.head: Bonds behaved differently.

segs.say: Bonds behaved differently. Their monthly correlation with shares was lower in 2020 and 2022 than over the whole period. Yet in 2022 the total-market fund lost 26.9% and the bond fund 13.0%: both had a bad year at once. Low correlation means the two didn’t move together month by month; it says nothing about whether both drift down over the same year. In 2022, rising interest rates pushed bond prices down steadily while shares fell for their own reasons. Correlation measures co-movement around each asset’s own average, not whether the averages themselves are positive.

scenes.head: Diversification reduces risk; it doesn’t guarantee anything

segs.say: Diversification reduces risk; it doesn’t guarantee anything. A 60/40 mix of the two funds still lost 21.3% in 2022 in the simulated history. Diversification makes bad outcomes less likely and less severe on average. It does not make shares safe for money needed soon, which is why Ana’s flat deposit, due in April 2032, stays in her savings account.

scenes.head: Sample covariance of two return series

segs.say: Sample covariance of two return series: cov(r_A, r_B) = 1/(n−1)Σₜ₌₁ⁿ(r_(A,t) − r̄_A)(r_(B,t) − r̄_B).
r_(A,t), r_(B,t): The two assets’ returns in period t (decimal).
r̄_A, r̄_B: Their mean returns over the sample (decimal).
n: Number of periods.
It assumes this: Both series cover the same periods. With scenarios, weight each product by its probability and drop the n − 1.
Excel: COVARIANCE.S. Monthly covariance × 12 is the annual covariance.

scenes.head: Correlation coefficient

segs.say: Correlation coefficient: ρ_(AB) = (cov(r_A, r_B))/(σ_A σ_B).
ρ_(AB): Correlation between A’s and B’s returns, from −1 to +1.
cov(r_A, r_B): Their covariance (decimal²).
σ_A, σ_B: Their standard deviations, in the same periods as the covariance (decimal).
It assumes this: Measures straight-line co-movement only.
Excel: CORREL. The same in monthly and annual units.

scenes.head: Expected return of a portfolio

segs.say: Expected return of a portfolio: E[r_P] = Σᵢ wᵢ E[rᵢ] two assets: E[r_P] = w E[r_A] + (1 − w) E[r_B].
wᵢ: Weight of holding i: its value ÷ the portfolio’s value; the weights sum to 1.
E[rᵢ]: Expected return of holding i (% per year).
It assumes this: Weights at the start of the period.

scenes.head: Standard deviation of a two-asset portfolio

segs.say: Standard deviation of a two-asset portfolio: σ_P = √(w²σ_A² + (1−w)²σ_B² + 2 w(1−w) ρ_(AB) σ_Aσ_B).
w: Weight in asset A (1 − w in B).
σ_A, σ_B: The assets’ standard deviations (% per year).
ρ_(AB): Their correlation.
It assumes this: Weights held constant (rebalanced each period).
ρσ_Aσ_B is the covariance, so the last term can be written 2w(1 − w)cov(r_A, r_B).

scenes.head: Minimum-variance weight for two assets

segs.say: Minimum-variance weight for two assets: w^* = (σ_B² − ρ_(AB)σ_Aσ_B)/(σ_A² + σ_B² − 2ρ_(AB)σ_Aσ_B).
w^*: Weight in A that gives the lowest portfolio variance.
σ_A, σ_B, ρ_(AB): As above.
It assumes this: Short selling allowed. If w* is below 0 or above 1 and short selling is not allowed, the least risky portfolio holds only the less risky asset.

scenes.head: Risk of an equally weighted portfolio of n assets

segs.say: Risk of an equally weighted portfolio of n assets: σ_P = √(1/n σ²̄ + (1 − 1/n)cov̄).
n: Number of holdings, each with weight 1/n.
σ²̄: Average variance of the holdings (decimal² per year).
cov̄: Average covariance between pairs of holdings (decimal² per year).
It assumes this: Uses averages; real holdings differ.
As n grows, σ_P falls towards √(average covariance): the systematic risk that remains.

chapters.title: Example: A ski resort and a beach hotel

scenes.head: A ski resort and a beach hotel

segs.say: Corrie Peak Ski Resort and Sandhaven Hotels are fictional listed companies. Analysts see three equally plausible kinds of season for next year, with these returns on the shares:

scenes.head: A ski resort and a beach hotel

segs.say: Step 1. Expected returns: Corrie Peak 0.3 × 20 + 0.4 × 10 + 0.3 × (−5) = 8.5%; Sandhaven 0.3 × 0 + 0.4 × 12 + 0.3 × 10 = 7.8%. Their standard deviations (square root of the probability-weighted squared deviations) are 9.76% and 5.17%.

Step 2. Deviations from the means, in percentage points: Corrie Peak 11.5, 1.5, −13.5; Sandhaven −7.8, 4.2, 2.2. Products: −89.7, 6.3, −29.7. Covariance = 0.3(−89.7) + 0.4(6.3) + 0.3(−29.7) = −33.3 (%²), or −0.00333 in decimals.
Step 3. Correlation: −0.00333 ÷ (0.0976 × 0.0517) = −0.66. The two tend to do well in different seasons.

Step 4. Half in each: the portfolio returns 10%, 11% and 2.5% in the three seasons. Expected return 0.3 × 10 + 0.4 × 11 + 0.3 × 2.5 = 8.15%; standard deviation 3.72%, against an average of the two standard deviations of 7.47%.

scenes.head: A ski resort and a beach hotel

segs.say: Covariance −0.00333, correlation −0.66; the 50/50 portfolio expects 8.15% with a standard deviation of 3.72%.

The portfolio’s expected return is exactly halfway between the two, but its risk is half the average: negative correlation lets each holding cushion the other’s bad season. The two-asset formula with ρ = −0.66 gives the same 3.72%.

chapters.title: Example: Shares and bonds for Ana: how much risk does a bond fund remove?

scenes.head: Shares and bonds for Ana: how much risk does a bond fund remove?

segs.say: From the simulated 2013–2027 history: the total-market fund has a mean of 10.43% and a standard deviation of 16.00% a year; the bond fund 4.31% and 4.14%; their correlation is 0.32. Find the expected return and standard deviation of a 60/40 mix, the risk saved by diversification, and the least risky mix with and without short selling.

scenes.head: Shares and bonds for Ana: how much risk does a bond fund remove?

segs.say: Step 3. Without diversification (ρ = 1) the standard deviation would be 0.6 × 16.00% + 0.4 × 4.14% = 11.25%; the saving is 1.00 point.
Step 5. Without short selling, the least risky portfolio is 100% bonds, with a standard deviation of 4.14%.

scenes.head: Shares and bonds for Ana: how much risk does a bond fund remove?

segs.say: 60/40: expected return 7.98%, standard deviation 10.25% (1.00 point below the 11.25% weighted average). The least risky long-only mix is all bonds.

Adding bonds to shares cuts risk faster than it cuts return: moving from 100% to 60% shares gives up 2.45 points of expected return and removes 5.75 points of standard deviation. Which mix suits Ana depends on how much risk she can bear, which the next lesson takes up. The figures are from simulated data.

chapters.title: Example: Two shares or one index fund?

scenes.head: Two shares or one index fund?

segs.say: Owen Marsh (fictional), a coffee wholesaler, wants to invest $20,000 in “businesses he understands”: half in Morrow & Pike Roasters and half in Harbour Street Foods. His adviser compares that with the total-market index fund, using the simulated 2013–2027 history (Morrow & Pike: 9.59% mean, 25.25% SD; Harbour Street: 12.53%, 32.03%; correlation 0.35; the fund: 10.43%, 16.00%).

scenes.head: Two shares or one index fund?

segs.say: Step 1. Two-share portfolio, expected return: 0.5 × 9.59% + 0.5 × 12.53% = 11.06%.

Step 2. Variance: 0.25 × 0.2525² plus 0.25 × 0.3203² plus 2 × 0.25 × 0.35 × 0.2525 × 0.3203 = 0.0558; standard deviation √0.0558 = 23.61%, below the 28.64% average of the two because the correlation is only 0.35.
Step 3. Compare with the fund: 0.63 points more mean return for 7.61 points more standard deviation. Fifteen years of simulated data cannot tell a mean difference that small from luck.
Step 4. Most of the extra risk is unsystematic: the formula for many holdings puts the floor for typical shares near 16.8%, so the extra 6.8 points or so comes from holding only two companies.

scenes.head: Two shares or one index fund?

segs.say: The two shares carry a standard deviation of about 23.6% a year against the fund’s 16.0%, for a mean return only 0.6 points higher in this sample.
The adviser’s point is not that the two companies are bad investments but that holding only two leaves risk the market does not pay for.

scenes.head: Ana’s two funds: every mix of shares and bonds

segs.say: Ana’s two funds, with the simulated means and standard deviations. Move the weight in shares and watch the expected return change in a straight line while the risk bends. Then drag the correlation: at 1 the curve becomes a straight line between the two funds; at −1 it touches zero risk. The slider starts at 0.30, the nearest step to the data’s 0.32. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: Two shares: Morrow & Pike and Harbour Street

segs.say: Two shares of similar risk, Morrow & Pike and Harbour Street. Find the least risky mix, then lower the correlation and see how much further the risk falls. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: Risk of an equally weighted portfolio of n typical shares

segs.say: How the risk of an equally weighted portfolio falls with the number of shares, and the floor it can’t pass. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: Averaging standard deviations

segs.say: Averaging standard deviations. A 60/40 portfolio’s standard deviation is not 60% of one plus 40% of the other unless the correlation is exactly 1. Use the two-asset formula; with Ana’s funds it gives 10.25%, not 11.25%. Expected returns, by contrast, do average.

scenes.head: Thinking more holdings always means much less risk

segs.say: Thinking more holdings always means much less risk. Adding holdings removes unsystematic risk only. Beyond a few dozen shares the gain is small, and the systematic risk that all shares share remains. Thirty shares in one industry diversify less than a broad index fund, because they share industry risk too.

scenes.head: Reading low correlation as protection in a bad year

segs.say: Reading low correlation as protection in a bad year. Correlation measures how two returns move around their own averages. Two assets with low correlation can both lose money over the same year, as the simulated shares and bonds did in 2022 (−26.9% and −13.0%).

scenes.head: Treating a correlation as a constant

segs.say: Treating a correlation as a constant. Correlations estimated from history change with the period and are noisy over short windows. Shares tend to become more correlated in crashes. Use a long sample, check how it varies, and don’t rely on a precise value.

scenes.head: Confusing covariance and correlation

segs.say: Confusing covariance and correlation. Covariance has units (per cent squared) and depends on how volatile the assets are, so its size says little by itself. Correlation divides by both standard deviations and lies between −1 and 1. Use covariance in the variance formula, correlation to judge how closely two assets move.

scenes.head: Ana’s fund choice.

segs.say: Ana’s fund choice. Ana’s first plan, everything in the total-market fund, is already diversified across the whole home share market: its 16.00% standard deviation is close to the floor for shares. What it can’t diversify is the market itself. Adding the bond fund, with its 0.32 correlation, is the cheapest way to lower risk, and the international fund adds a little more diversification across economies. How much of each she should hold depends on her horizon and on how large a fall she could live with: that is the subject of the next lesson.

scenes.head: A pension committee’s review.

segs.say: A pension committee’s review. The trustees of a fictional company pension plan review their asset mix every year. Their consultant reports each asset class’s expected return and standard deviation and the correlations between them, then the portfolio’s standard deviation from the full covariance matrix (the many-asset version of the formula above). She also shows the correlations measured over the worst months, because the trustees care most about whether the mix holds up in a crash.

scenes.head: Employees and their employer’s shares.

segs.say: Employees and their employer’s shares. A fictional battery-storage installer offers staff shares at a discount. An employee who puts most of her savings into them doubles up on one company’s risk: if the firm struggles she could lose her job and her savings together, so her savings and her income are highly correlated. A financial planner would suggest keeping that holding small and spreading the rest across broad funds.

scenes.head: What to remember

segs.say: A portfolio’s expected return is the weighted average of its holdings’ expected returns; its standard deviation is below the weighted average whenever the correlation is below 1.
Covariance is the average product of deviations from the means; correlation divides it by both standard deviations and runs from −1 to +1.
Two assets: σ_P² = w²σ_A² + (1 − w)²σ_B² + 2w(1 − w)ρσ_Aσ_B. Ana’s 60/40 mix of the simulated funds: 7.98% expected return, 10.25% standard deviation.
The minimum-variance weight can be negative; without short selling the least risky portfolio may hold only the safer asset, as with Ana’s shares and bonds.
Adding holdings removes unsystematic risk; systematic risk, the average covariance, remains. Most of the gain comes from the first ten or so shares.
Correlations change: in the simulated crashes shares moved together more. Low correlation doesn’t stop two assets both losing over a year, as shares and bonds did in 2022.

scenes.head: Work the guided problems, then take the knowledge check.

segs.say: That is the whole lesson. Now work the guided problems, with hints when you need them, then try the questions on your own and take the knowledge check. A score of 80 percent completes the lesson.
